why/slow: Training a model takes many gradient steps, and every step needs the gradients of a whole batch of examples. One chip working through them all alone, step after step, is slow.
why/gpu: That chip is a GPU, a graphics processing unit: first built to draw graphics, it does many multiplications at once.
why/copies: So share the work. Give each of several GPUs a full copy of the weights, w: every one of its numbers, called the parameters.
why/slice: And give each its own slice of the batch: a hundred and twenty eight examples, split four ways, is thirty two each.
why/G: Call the number of GPUs G. Turned around, G slices of thirty two make the batch: four times thirty two, a hundred and twenty eight.
why/name: The data is split, the weights are copied, and the GPUs work in parallel, at the same time. That is data parallelism. Each GPU has a quarter of the work.
why/goyal: In 2017, Priya Goyal and colleagues trained on over a million images this way, with two hundred and fifty six GPUs at thirty two images each. Training that had taken twenty nine hours on eight GPUs took one hour.
average/loss: Training makes a function, f, small: f measures how badly the weights do on the examples, and is called the loss.
average/grad: Each GPU works out the gradient of the loss on its own slice, the average over its thirty two examples, all four at once. GPU zero's is written g zero, GPU one's g one, and so on.
average/per: For one weight, the four might find two, minus one, three and zero. Different slices give different gradients.
average/mean: So they send them to each other and average: they add up to four, and four over four is one.
average/whole: The slices are the same size, so this average of four averages is the average over all a hundred and twenty eight examples: exactly the gradient of the whole batch.
average/vec: Every other weight is averaged the same way, entry by entry: its own four gradients, one from each GPU.
average/step: Then every GPU takes the same step with that same average, so the copies stay identical. With their own gradients, they would drift apart.
average/send: So each step, what travels between the GPUs is gradients: one number per parameter, from every GPU. The examples stay put, and the loss, a single number, could not say which way to move each weight.
epoch/epoch: An epoch is still one pass through all N examples: here, twelve thousand eight hundred.
epoch/step: And a step still takes one whole batch, all four slices at once: a hundred and twenty eight examples.
epoch/steps: So an epoch takes N over B steps: twelve thousand eight hundred over a hundred and twenty eight is a hundred.
epoch/not: Not four hundred. The four slices are worked at the same time, so together they make one step, not four.
epoch/more: With eight GPUs at thirty two each, the batch is two hundred and fifty six: fifty steps, each covering twice the data.
